# Transmission, outbreaks and One Health

> *A pathogen that cannot reach a new host dies with the one it is in. This chapter asks the fourth
> question of the book: where does a microbe live, and how does it travel? The answer explains both
> how outbreaks behave and where they can be interrupted.*

## The chain of infection {#sec-trans-chain}

Transmission is usually described as a chain of six links. Each link is a place the chain can be
broken, which is why the model is worth learning as a checklist rather than a list of words.

| Link | What it means | Example of breaking it |
|---|---|---|
| **Reservoir** | Where the organism normally lives and multiplies: people, animals, soil or water | Treating infected people; vector control |
| **Portal of exit** | How it leaves the reservoir: respiratory particles, faeces, blood, skin | Covering coughs; wound dressings |
| **Mode of transmission** | How it travels (below) | Hand hygiene; safe water; mosquito control |
| **Portal of entry** | How it enters the next host: mouth, airway, broken skin, mucosa | Gloves; safe injection practice |
| **Susceptible host** | A person able to be infected | Vaccination |
| **Infectious agent** | The organism itself | Antimicrobial treatment; sterilisation |

**Reservoirs** differ in a way that matters for control. An organism whose only reservoir is humans
can in principle be eradicated: smallpox was, and polio is close. An organism with an animal or
environmental reservoir cannot be, because it persists whatever happens in the human population.

A **zoonosis** is an infection transmitted from animals to humans. Around 60% of known human
infectious diseases and about 75% of emerging ones have an animal origin [@taylor2001risk]. A
**vector** is an arthropod that carries an organism between hosts, usually a mosquito, tick, flea or
louse. A **fomite** is an inanimate object that carries organisms, such as a door handle or a shared
keyboard.

## Routes of transmission {#sec-trans-routes}

<div data-island="sorter" data-src="/diagrams/transmission-sorter.yml"></div>

Two points about the respiratory route are worth stating, because the distinction was argued over
publicly during the COVID-19 pandemic. Particles breathed out span a continuous range of sizes. Large
ones fall to the ground within a short distance; small ones evaporate and stay suspended, so they
accumulate in poorly ventilated rooms and can infect people further away. The older teaching, which
split these into two separate categories with a fixed size cut-off, is now recognised as too rigid
[@wang2021airborne]. For control, what matters is distance, time and ventilation.

## Measuring how an infection spreads {#sec-trans-measures}

Four quantities describe transmission. Each answers a different question.

| Quantity | Question it answers | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Incubation period** | How long between infection and symptoms? | Sets how long contacts are observed |
| **Infectious period** | When can this person pass it on? | May start before symptoms, which makes control much harder |
| **Basic reproduction number, R₀** | How many people does one case infect in a fully susceptible population? | A property of the organism *and* the population, not of the organism alone |
| **Effective reproduction number, R** | How many does one case infect now, given immunity and control measures? | R > 1: cases grow. R < 1: the outbreak shrinks |

Because R falls as immunity rises, there is a threshold above which an outbreak cannot sustain
itself. If a fraction of the population is immune, the **herd immunity threshold** is 1 − 1/R₀. For
an organism with R₀ of 2, that is 50%; for a highly transmissible one with R₀ of 12, it is above 90%,
which is why measles requires such high vaccination coverage.

<div data-island="epidemic-sim" data-src="/diagrams/epidemic-sim.yml"></div>

Three features of the model are worth noticing because they are general. The outbreak stops while
susceptible people remain: transmission falls below replacement before everyone has been infected.
Reducing transmission lowers the peak *and* delays it, which is the reasoning behind measures
intended to keep demand within hospital capacity. And a small change in R₀ makes a large difference
to the final size, because the effect compounds.

## Investigating an outbreak {#sec-trans-outbreak}

An **outbreak** is more cases of a disease than expected in a place and time. **Endemic** means
constantly present in a population; **epidemic** means a sharp rise above that baseline; **pandemic**
means an epidemic across many countries.

Investigation follows a standard sequence: confirm that the cases are real and define what counts
as a case; describe the cases by **person, place and time**; use that description to generate a
hypothesis about the source; test the hypothesis by comparing exposures between people who became
ill and people who did not; and act to interrupt transmission. Action does not wait for certainty.

The shape of an **epidemic curve**, a plot of cases against time of onset, carries information.
Cases that cluster within one incubation period suggest a single shared exposure, as in the wedding
lunch in the *Gram-positive cocci* chapter. Cases spread over successive incubation periods, each
wave larger, suggest spread from person to person.

## Hand hygiene: the evidence came first {#sec-trans-semmelweis}

In the Vienna General Hospital in the 1840s, two maternity clinics had very different death rates
from puerperal fever, the infection that follows childbirth. In the clinic staffed by medical
students, who came to deliveries from the autopsy room, mortality ran several times higher than in
the midwives' clinic [@semmelweis1861]. Ignaz Semmelweis reasoned that something was being carried on
hands from the dead to the living, and required staff to wash in chlorinated lime. Deaths fell
sharply.

He could not say what was being carried, germ theory being decades away, and his colleagues largely
rejected the finding. The episode makes the same point as Snow's pump: an interruptible route is
enough to act on. It is also why hand hygiene remains the single most effective measure against
healthcare-associated infection.

## One Health {#sec-trans-onehealth}

**One Health** is the principle that human, animal and environmental health are interdependent, and
that infections are best understood and controlled across all three. The connections are practical
rather than abstract:

- Most emerging infections come from animals, so surveillance in animals gives earlier warning.
- Antimicrobials used in animals select resistant bacteria that reach people through food, water and
  direct contact.
- Changes in land use, climate and travel alter where vectors can live and which animals humans meet.

Singapore shows the approach in several forms. Dengue control works on the vector, including the
release of male mosquitoes carrying *Wolbachia*. Hand, foot and mouth disease surveillance covers
childcare centres, where asymptomatic carriage is common. The 1999 Nipah virus outbreak was traced
to pigs imported from Malaysia and was controlled by acting on the animal side. Melioidosis comes
from soil and surface water, and cases rise after heavy rain.
